Shopify and Web Design

How Long Does It Take to Build a Website

By Marie Glow StudioPublished September 18, 2026

A simple one page website can go live in about five business days once content is ready, while a full brand identity paired with a multi page site usually takes two to three weeks. What matters most to the timeline is how quickly the business owner supplies content, photos and decisions.

Most delays on a website project are not design problems. They are waiting problems, waiting on a logo file, waiting on product photos, waiting on a decision about wording. Understanding that in advance is the fastest way to keep a project on schedule.

How long does a simple one page website take?

About five business days from a completed intake, for a straightforward one page site with existing branding and ready content. This works well for a shop or service business that needs one clear page with services, trust, contact and a call to action, not a large multi page structure.

How long does a full multi page website take?

Roughly two to three weeks for a custom multi page build that includes a brand identity, a homepage, several supporting pages, product or service organization and a full review before launch. This range still depends heavily on how quickly content, images and approvals come back during the process.

What happens during each phase of a website build?

Most builds move through the same rough phases, whether the site is one page or many: intake and planning, where scope and content get confirmed; design, where the layout and look come together; build, where the actual pages get put together and connected; and review, where the owner checks everything on a real phone and desktop before launch. A one page site moves through all four quickly since there is less to design and build. A multi page site with a full brand identity spends more time in design, since the logo, colors and style guide have to be settled before the pages can be built around them.

What actually slows a website build down?

  1. Missing or incomplete copy for key pages
  2. Product or service photos that still need to be taken or gathered
  3. Undecided branding, such as colors, fonts or a logo
  4. Slow turnaround on approving drafts or answering questions
  5. Adding new pages or features after the project has started
  6. Waiting on domain access or account logins needed to connect the site

How can a business owner speed things up?

Prepare as much as possible before the project starts. Gathering the essentials up front turns most of the timeline into design and build time instead of back and forth.

  • Finalize copy, or at least rough notes, for every planned page
  • Collect final photos, sized reasonably and in focus
  • Settle on colors, fonts and a logo if the brand already has one
  • List services or products with prices, descriptions and any variants
  • Have domain and account access ready to hand over when asked
  • Set aside time to review drafts quickly rather than letting them sit

Does the platform affect how long a website takes?

Somewhat, but less than most people expect. Shopify, for a store, and a custom-coded build, for a service business without e-commerce needs, both move at a similar pace once content is ready, because the platform mainly affects what is possible, not how fast pages get built. The real time difference comes from scope: number of pages, amount of custom design and how much content still needs to be written or gathered.

How many revision rounds should a website include?

Enough for the owner to catch real problems, without turning into an open-ended redesign. A single revision round after the first draft is common for a smaller project, covering wording changes, image swaps and small layout adjustments. Requests that change the scope, such as adding new pages or a different structure partway through, usually reset the timeline rather than fitting inside the original revision round.

What happens if content is not ready on time?

The timeline moves with it. A designer working from a written scope, such as a five business day guarantee, is usually counting from a completed intake, meaning the clock starts once the needed information arrives, not when the project is booked. How Much Does a Small Business Website Cost covers how that same scope also drives price.

Does the time of year affect a website timeline?

Indirectly, through demand rather than the calendar itself. A designer or agency may book up before a busy retail season, so a business that waits until the last minute to start a project can find the earliest available start date is later than the stated turnaround. Starting the intake process early protects against that kind of scheduling delay, separate from the build time itself.

How should a business owner plan around the timeline?

Avoid booking a website build right before a launch, event or busy season unless there is real buffer time. Building in a week or two of slack protects against a normal delay, like a slow photo shoot, a late branding decision or a busy week that pushes a review back, without putting a hard deadline at risk.

Frequently asked questions

How fast can a small business website go live?

A simple one page site can go live in about five business days once all content is ready. A full multi page build with branding typically takes two to three weeks.

What causes most website delays?

Waiting on the business owner's content, photos, branding decisions or approvals, far more often than the design or build work itself.

Can a website be built faster with a bigger budget?

Sometimes, but content readiness usually matters more than budget. A rushed build with unclear content and photos rarely turns out well regardless of price.

When should a business start a website project before a launch?

Earlier than the minimum timeline suggests, with a week or two of buffer for normal delays like photo shoots, copy revisions or slow approvals.
